newsitem.title: USA: Thanksgiving a nightmare for friends of the turkey.
newsitem.headline: Thanksgiving a nightmare for friends of the turkey.

text.p: America's Thanksgiving Day holiday, when tens of millions of turkeys are roasted for dinner, is the worst day of the year for the people at United Poultry Concerns.

While President Bill Clinton joined festive preparations for Thursday's family feasting, saying that "45 million turkeys will pay the supreme sacrifice for our Thanksgiving," the people at UPC winced and spoke of the turkey as victim.

Karen Davis, president and founder of the nonprofit group based outside Washington, got ready for a strictly vegetarian banquet. The days leading up to her Thanksgiving were devoted to raising the public consciousness and protesting.
Thanksgiving "glorifies everything I don't believe in," Davis said as she prepared a morning meal for the 32 chickens and two turkeys who live in a "sanctuary" next to her kitchen.
"I'm cooking a big kettle full of rice and corn for the chickens, because it's so cold," she said as a rooster crowed.

The holiday, on the last Thursday of November each year, originated in the early 17th century, when English settlers gave thanks for their survival in the new American colonies, where wild turkey was one of the tastiest available foods.

Davis questioned "the mockery of turkeys that seems to accompany the sentimentality around Thanksgiving." The sentimentality "seems to be countered by a pathological need to ridicule the centrepiece victim of the piece," she said.

To protest against what they call cruel poultry-raising techniques, Davis and about 30 other activists attempted on Tuesday to hold a candlelight vigil outside a Maryland turkey farm, but high winds blew out the candles.

Davis's nonprofit group held an vegetarian potluck dinner on Sunday, attended by humans and assorted poultry. Story time featured the tale of "how eight school children rescue eight fluffy turkeys from Farmer Mack Nugget on Thanksgiving Eve."

To further her group's vision of the holiday, Davis has put together an alternative Thanksgiving menu consisting of pastry-wrapped nut loaf, mushroom gravy, rosemary roast potatoes, stuffed squash, braised vegetables and apple tart.

Davis, for whom UPC is a full-time occupation, said she was galvanised to act by a chicken she named Viva, one of several formerly in a chicken house near her home. Davis came to see Viva as a companion who could take part in a dialogue.
Her 6-year-old group produces a quarterly newsletter, Poultry Press, that carries children's odes to their poultry pets and decries such events as ostrich-drawn chariot races.
Davis has written a book of recipes, one on the poultry industry and "A Home for Henny," for children and part of a campaign to replace chicken-hatching projects in classrooms.
Meanwhile in Washington, Clinton, a carnivore famed for his big appetite, did something that, if it were not an isolated act, might have stirred a flicker of hope in Davis.

Upholding a White House tradition, he formally spared the life of a 65-pound bird in a ceremony in the White House Rose Garden. Presented by the National Turkey Federation and named Carl, the bird will go to a petting zoo.
